title: Outer and Inner Self: The Path to Eternal Glory
speaker: Unknown Speaker
summary: This message explores Paul's dual motivation for not losing heart: the greatness of the new covenant and the glory of heaven. The speaker teaches that distinguishing between outer self (physical body) and inner self (soul/spirit) is crucial for spiritual endurance, using examples of transgenderism, addiction, and anxiety to demonstrate how inner self issues must be addressed spiritually rather than merely physically.

transcript:
## What Motivates You to Keep Going?

What motivates you to keep going? There must be something that motivates you to keep going with life. Is it your paycheck? Is it the weekend? TGIF? Is that your model for life? Is it fear that motivates you? Is it the love of family that motivates you? Is it the love of God that motivates you? Motivation is often, if not always, a mixed bag that propels us forward. There are good things and there are things that are not so good.

Paul's motivation to keep going in his calling as a pastor to the Corinthians was twofold. In verse one of chapter four, we learned that he did not quit and he did not lose heart because of the greatness of the new covenant of which he was a minister. Then we see in this passage today, in verses 16 through 18, that heaven was extraordinarily attractive to him. The path to heaven went through fulfilling God's calling in his life. That is why he would not quit and why he would not lose heart. It is of this second motivation, the glory of heaven, that we speak about today.

## The Text: 2 Corinthians 4:16-18

Look at verses 16 through 18 once again:

> Therefore, do not lose heart. Though our outward man is perishing, yet our inward man is being renewed day by day; for our light affliction, which is but for a moment, is working for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. For we do not look at the things which are seen but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

Why would we not look at the things which are seen but at the things which are not seen? Because the things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

Last week, like the golden hammer metaphor, we attempted to extract three points from the text, but only two came out. So we have two main points from our passage.

## Point One: Distinguishing Outer Self from Inner Self Prevents Us from Losing Heart

### Understanding the Outer Self and Inner Self

The first point is this: knowing what is an outer self issue and what is an inner self issue helps us not give up in life and in service to Christ.

Paul returns to the theme of verse one—do not lose heart, we do not lose heart, we do not quit. One of the reasons he does not quit is because even though the outer self, the outer man is decaying, the inner man is being renewed day by day.

The outer man is the physical body. Our physical bodies are wasting away. All of us are moving toward death, and that is the inescapable path for everyone unless the Lord returns. As we age, our bodies are not able to do things that they once could. Our bodies decay. We are often not good stewards of our bodies, and they decay because of that. We also live in a sinner's world, so diseases ravage our bodies. Our own sinful actions done in our bodies cause our bodies to decay. Things that other people do to us can affect our bodies. So we understand what Paul is saying when he says that the outer man is decaying, that the outer self, the physical body is decaying. This is an undeniable truth that we see in our own lives.

### The Inner Man Can Be Renewed Despite Physical Decay

The next thing that Paul says is more counterintuitive. Even when our bodies are decaying, our souls—that immaterial part, our spiritual self, our heart—all of these are synonyms and mean the same thing—can continue to grow and become more and more alive. Paul says that even though the outer man, the physical body is perishing, the inner man is being renewed day by day. This aligns with what Paul said at the end of chapter 3, that in Christ we are growing from glory to glory. Even as our bodies decay, our souls are able to soar to heaven.

Now, the outer man and the inner man, the outer self and the inner self are connected and they affect each other. But physical decline or physical suffering do not necessitate spiritual decline. This is true even with people who suffer from dementia, which is an outer man, a physical issue. Even people who suffer from dementia can continue to be renewed by the Spirit of God through the Word that can penetrate even the impenetrable.

We tend to think that our minds and our brains are the same thing, but they are not. The brain is the hardware; the mind is the interface. That interface can still be accessed through the Word of God, even if we cannot tell from outward appearances.

Remember, brothers and sisters, the Word of God according to the Scriptures is living and powerful and sharper than a two-edged sword:

> It pierces even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

Even when the outer man gives no indication that anything is present, even then the inner man can grow through the Word of God and be renewed day by day.

### Inner Self Issues Cannot Be Solved by Physical Means

Brothers and sisters, we are now going to address some uncomfortable truths. This is rare for me, I know. We have been taught that everything today can be explained in terms of biology, which is a false explanation because we are not just body—we are body and soul.

In Aldous Huxley's dystopian novel "Brave New World," he predicted a future in which everything would be solved by medication. George Orwell, writing at the same time, predicted that everything would be resolved by government. But Huxley was a visionary because that is where we are today. Even in the Church of Jesus Christ, we forget that we are body and soul, and we think that everything can be solved biologically and medically. That is not what the Scriptures teach.

This verse teaches us that our bodies cannot make us sin. If the Bible says something is sin, it remains a sin regardless of potential difficulties our bodies may put in the way of obeying God. Sin is always, always in the domain of the inner self. We confuse things in a very unhelpful way when we attribute inner self issues to the outer self, when we attribute soul and heart issues to the physical body and to the physical realm.

Let me give you three concrete examples of inner self issues that are often attributed to the body.

### Example One: Transgenderism

The first example is transgenderism. Our culture has accepted the idea that the way to help a person with inner self struggles about their sexual identity is by mutilating the body, making the inner self issue an outer man issue. The Scriptures clearly teach that sexual confusion is an inner man issue. In Romans 1, verses 24 to 27, the Apostle Paul says:

> God also gave them up to uncleanness in the lusts of their hearts to dishonor their bodies among themselves, who exchanged the truth of God for the lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever, Amen. For this reason God gave them up to vile passions. For even their women exchanged the natural use for what is against nature. Likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of a woman, burned in their lust for one another, men with men committing what is shameful and receiving in themselves the penalty of their error which was due.

Transgender issues are worship issues, not body issues. Once we consider the issues in their proper realms, we are able to deal with our hearts and help others who are struggling with them.

Consider this analogy. If a young woman—or these days, the percentage is almost similar for a young man—comes to you and they are skin and bones, labeled with anorexia nervosa (a condition where the person thinks they are always fatter than they actually are), medically sick with a wasting body, and they say, "Oh, I think I am so fat," what would you tell them? Would you say, "Yes, I think you should go on a diet or get bariatric surgery"? No. You would say, "That is not true. There is something wrong with your thinking, not with your body." Yet when someone says, "I think I was born in the wrong body," we say, "Go cut yourself up." Do you see the discrepancy? That is what happens when we make an inner man issue an outer man issue.

### Example Two: Addiction

Let us move to something a bit closer to home. The second issue is addiction. Addiction is an inner man issue, not an outer man issue. The Bible teaches that addiction, better thought of as enslavement, is an inner man issue.

Our Savior says:

> Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

I have talked to people who are addicted, husband and wife, and the wife gives an ultimatum: "If you do not stop, I will leave you." The husband's answer was, "I love this thing more than I love you, and I am going to choose my addiction." That is an inner person issue.

In Proverbs 9, verses 13 through 18, we have this picture of the foolish woman calling people into her house:

> A foolish woman is clamorous; she is simple and knows nothing. For she sits at the door of her house on the seat by the highest place of the city to call those who pass by, who go straight on their way: "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here." And as for him who lacks understanding, she says to him, "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of hell.

What she is inviting them into is a banquet in the grave. That is what addictions are.

James asks in James chapter 4:

> Where do wars and fights come among you? Do they not come from your desires for pleasure, that war in your members?

That is the place where these enslavements that we call addictions come from—the heart. It is true that some addictions involving substances have a physical component. But at their core, addiction is idolatrous self-enslavement. If you have been chemically dependent, you know that after 21 days your body is no longer chemically dependent on whatever substance it is. But you also know that even after that chemical has left your body, you crave it intensely. That has nothing to do with the physical aspect—that has to do with our heart.

Addiction is not ultimately a medical issue, though substances do ravage our body and we might need medical attention. It is an issue of heart worship. If we keep it that way, we are able to overcome addictions and help those who are enslaved to it. Christ is the best solution for addictions. The sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit in the inner man is the best solution for addictions.

### Example Three: Anxiety

Now our third example. Our culture now teaches that anxiety is a medical issue. The Bible teaches clearly that anxiety is an inner man issue. We know the passages. In Philippians 4, verses 6 and following, the Apostle says:

> Be anxious for nothing. But in everything, by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God; and the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds through Christ Jesus.

What mode, what tense, what language is being used here when Paul says, "Be anxious for nothing"? Is there a suggestion? Is that an opinion? Is that a command? It is a command. And if we do not do that, remember, sin is any lack of conformity to what the Word of God says. We are sinning.

Our Savior in Matthew chapter 6, starting at verse 25, says:

> Therefore I say to you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink; nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food and the body more than clothing? Which of you by worrying can add one cubit to his stature? So why do you worry about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin; and yet I say to you that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. Now if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will He not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?

Jesus makes anxiety an issue of faith. Was He misguided? Was He saying, "Hang on until the 1950s and in 2,000 years someone is going to come up with a medicine that will take care of this"? Was He unaware that there would be drugs later on? He says:

> Therefore do not worry, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For after all these things the Gentiles seek. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things.

Yet anti-anxiety medications are among the most prescribed in the United States. But anxiety should not be dealt with medically as an outer man issue but through the grace of God in Christ as an inner man issue.

### The Relationship Between Outer and Inner Self

Brothers and sisters, I am not saying that outer man issues do not affect the inner man or that inner man issues do not affect our outer man. After all, we are a unit. We are not two people. We are one unit. What I am saying is that we need to place the origin of the issue in the right sphere if we want to deal with it effectively for the glory of God and for the good of the people we are trying to help and for our own good as we deal with these issues.

I bet if I asked you to raise your hand if you have ever been anxious, all our hands would go up, including mine. I have had panic attacks. I struggle with it at times. But the answer is not in the body. The answer is in the heart, through the work of the Spirit, through the ministry of the Word of God, through the community of Christ coming alongside us and helping us to see a greater Christ than the one we are currently seeing.

The most compassionate thing is to call inner man issues inner man issues, because inner man issues are sanctification issues. They are opportunities for us to grow in Christ. So Paul does not lose heart because no matter what anyone does to his body, his soul can still soar to the heights of heaven.

That is the experience of the Psalmist in Psalm 119. For example, in verse 71, the Psalmist says:

> It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn Your statutes.

In verse 92:

> Unless Your law had been my delight, I would then have perished in my affliction.

Notice that in both cases the inner issue remained an inner man issue, and there was growth through the Word of God. So Paul does not lose heart because no matter what the Corinthians do to him, as his outer man wastes away, the inner man continues to grow.

## Point Two: Proper Perspective on Outer and Inner Self Makes Heaven Precious to Us

### Heaven Becomes More Desirable Through Affliction

Secondly, knowing what is an outer man issue and what is an inner man issue makes heaven much more precious to us. Keeping things where they belong makes heaven much more precious to us. See that in verses 17 and 18 where Paul says:

> For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, is working for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory. While we do not look at the things which are seen but at the things which are not seen; for the things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

When outer and inner man issues are in the proper place, we are better able to long for heaven while laboring for heaven in this life. Our afflictions are not earning heaven for us. Though some of us see them that way—like, "Oh, I need to suffer because I have been so bad and I need to atone for myself before God." That does not happen. Our afflictions are not earning us heaven. They are preparing us by producing a much greater expectation for eternity.

Our sufferings now make us crave heaven and long for it. It looks more beautiful. Christ looks more beautiful, greater, more attractive. Eternity looks much better as we go through afflictions here. It builds a great expectation for eternity—an expectation that cannot be disappointed.

Brothers and sisters, you can never think of Christ too much. Whatever you can imagine, glory will be much greater than that. Our bodily afflictions, if seen properly, cause us to crave eternal glory even more. Not in a morbid way, not in a way that we are going to take our lives away, but the afflictions of this life magnify heaven in our eyes. It helps us take our eyes from this life and put them on the life to come.

This life's affliction is temporary; heaven's glory is eternal, as the apostle says in these two verses. The glory that Paul is looking forward to is resurrection glory—the glory that we cannot see now but will see at the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ. The author of Hebrews tells us that that is the essence of faith:

> Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

I want you to understand that Paul is not minimizing human suffering. I have been in ministry for 27 years as an ordained pastor. I have come across a lot of different sufferings. You hear stories that would make the angels of heaven weep. Yet Paul says that even then, those are temporary, momentary afflictions. So we do not want to minimize human suffering. We should always be compassionate. But he is, however, putting things in perspective. Compared to eternity, even the deepest suffering is light and momentary.

Do you believe that? In the parallel passage in Romans chapter 8, Paul says:

> The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. For the earnest expectation of the creation eagerly waits for the revealing of the sons of God, for the creation was subjected to futility not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it in hope. Because the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God, for we know that the whole creation groans and labors with birth pangs together until now. Not only that, but we also who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves, groan within ourselves, eagerly waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body.

### Suffering as Labor Pains Leading to Resurrection

What Paul is saying is that what we live today in this life is that moment in labor where the pangs are the most intense. This life is intense and painful. But it is not hopeless. It is in the hope that in a few moments there will be a child in your arms—a gift from God. That is what we are experiencing now. The afflictions of this life can prepare us for the life to come by doing at least three things.

First, they show that we are weak. Nothing makes you feel less powerful, more powerless than seeing your child suffer and being unable to relieve that suffering. That shows how weak we truly are.

Second, afflictions remove self-reliance. When we know we cannot help ourselves, we stop trusting in ourselves.

Third, they help us to look up, not around. We have already looked around and there is no solution for our affliction. So we have to look up. As someone said, flat on your back is the best way to see heaven because you can only look up. That is what afflictions do for us. They show we are weak, they remove self-reliance, and they help us to look up, not around.

And afflictions help us not to hope in the things of this world. They help us to hope in things that are not seen—things of the world to come and things that are part of Christ's kingdom. Afflictions have a way of making us see better. They are the perfect glasses for us to see life as it really is. They are good for us because the things of this world will pass away. They are transient. They help us see that.

What is not seen today will be seen at the return of the Lord Jesus Christ when we are raised from the dead to be with Him.

## Six Reasons to Look Forward to the Life to Come

Why is the life to come something to look forward to? I am going to give you six reasons, all from Revelation 21 and 22.

**First**, the dwelling place of God will be with men. (Revelation 21:3)

**Second**, God Himself will be with us, which is the fulfillment of all the promises of the Bible. (Revelation 21:3)

**Third**, there will be no tears, no suffering—only tears of joy. (Revelation 21:4)

**Fourth**, there will be no death, no separation. (Revelation 21:4)

**Fifth**, there will be no mourning, no crying, no pain. (Revelation 21:4)

**Sixth**, the curse of the fall will be gone. (Revelation 21:22-23)

**And the best reason**: Jesus will be there. We will see Him as He is, for we will be like Him. (Revelation 21:5-6)

## How Should We Live?

If all this is true—and it is—how should it affect the way we live? Let me offer four suggestions.

### First: Interpret Your Struggles Correctly

Interpret your struggles correctly. Distinguish body from heart. In your daily life, train yourself to ask, "Is this primarily an outer man issue or an inner man issue?"

### Second: Prioritize Inner Renewal over Outward Comfort

Prioritize inner renewal over outward comfort. Your schedule often reveals what you value most. This passage calls you to invest more intentionally in the inner man because that is eternal.

### Third: Respond to Suffering with Eternal Perspective

Respond to suffering with eternal perspective, not despair. When difficulties come—whether relational conflicts, financial strains, or physical pain—interpret them through eternity. Remember that compared to eternity, they are light and they are momentary.

### Fourth: Let Eternity Shape Your Relationships and Priorities

Let eternity shape your relationships and priorities. If unseen eternal realities are more important than visible temporary ones, that should change the way you treat people. Why? Because things are temporary, but people are eternal. That should help us shape our priorities in life.

## Conclusion

It all boils down to this: Live in a way that shows you truly believe what cannot yet be seen. Live in a way that shows you truly believe that this is not our best life. It is still to come at the return of the Lord Jesus Christ.
